content:
China - Superconducting magnetic propulsion device for spacecraft patent 

#ufotwitter

It is a propellant-free (no working medium) propulsion system that generates thrust by interacting with a planet's natural magnetic field. 

Key components:

Superconducting coil unit (cooled by liquid helium to maintain superconductivity)

Magnetic field measurement module

Acceleration measurement module

Control and power modules
Liquid helium refrigeration system (using a Stirling refrigerator)

Idea uses local magnetic shielding via the Meissner effect in superconducting materials. This creates an asymmetry: the ampere forces (Lorentz forces) on different parts of the coil don't fully cancel out when the device moves through a non-uniform or varying planetary magnetic field. 

It was filed in 2018 by researchers at Nanjing University of Aeronautics and Astronautics (China) and granted in 2021.

Why it's unconventional

Most spacecraft propulsion relies on expelling mass (chemical rockets, ion thrusters, cold gas, etc.) — this one uses no propellant at all and draws energy from the interaction with the ambient planetary magnetic field.

Traditional magnetic sails or magnetoplasmadynamic thrusters are usually much larger, have stronger external magnetic fields, and are more suited to interplanetary space or solar wind. This design is compact, low-interference, and intended for low Earth orbit or inside habitats.

It exploits subtle differences in the magnetic field (gradients or variations as the spacecraft orbits) rather than generating its own strong field for propulsion in the usual sense.

Applicability to strong-field environments like Jupiter is highlighted, which is niche but interesting for future missions.

In short: it's a propellantless electromagnetic propulsion concept relying on superconductivity and clever shielding — more in the realm of advanced/exotic space propulsion research than mainstream technology.

This is just one of many official American, Russian, and Chinese state patents on an unconventional propulsion system.
